name: Eastern DR Congo war (M23/AFC, now FRN, vs Kinshasa)
started: 2025-01-27 (M23 capture of Goma; M23 resurgence began in late 2021)
summary: Rwanda-backed M23 rebels hold Goma, Bukavu and much of North and South Kivu after their 2025 offensive, and briefly took Uvira in December 2025 before withdrawing under US pressure. Since then a FARDC-Burundian-Wazalendo coalition, backed by Chinese and Turkish drones and Western contractors, has been fighting M23 to a bloody stalemate on several axes. On 12 Oct 2026 former president Joseph Kabila became leader of a rebranded M23 political front, the FRN, which vowed to topple Tshisekedi by force.

sides.name: DRC government coalition
members: Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC), incl. 'Black Mambas' special forces
Private military contractors: Vectus Global (Erik Prince), Colombian mercenaries
backers: Turkey and China (TAI Anka, TB2 alleged, CH-4 drones supplied)
United States (diplomatic and economic leverage via the Washington accords and sanctions on Rwanda and M23 figures)
sides.strength: No reliable current FARDC/Wazalendo figure found. Burundi had about 18,000 troops in South Kivu before Uvira fell (CTP, Dec 2025); about 4,000-5,000 fighting alongside FARDC in Feb-Apr 2026 (Wikipedia timeline).

sides.name: M23 / AFC, rebranded FRN from 12 Oct 2026
members: March 23 Movement (M23) and its army, the ARC
Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC), political wing until Oct 2026
Front pour la Refondation de la Nation (FRN)
backers: Rwanda: Rwanda Defence Force troops, command support and logistics (UN assessments; Rwanda acknowledged 'security coordination' with AFC/M23 in Jan 2026)
leaders: Joseph Kabila (FRN president, former DRC president)
Gen. Sultani Makenga (ARC chief of staff)
sides.strength: About 30,000 combatants (UN Group of Experts, June 2026), possibly approaching 40,000 after a July 2026 graduation of 9,318 recruits (unverified, KT Press). RDF in DRC: 3,000-4,000 (UN, 2024) to 4,000-7,000 (2025 estimate cited by Wikipedia).

background: M23 is a mainly Congolese Tutsi rebel movement that first seized Goma in 2012 and re-emerged in late 2021. UN experts have repeatedly found that Rwanda commands and supports its operations, which Kigali frames as defence against the FDLR, a militia descended from perpetrators of the 1994 genocide. In January and February 2025 M23 and Rwandan forces captured Goma and Bukavu, the capitals of North and South Kivu, and set up parallel administrations, financed partly by the Rubaya coltan mines (about 15% of world supply; at least US$800,000 a month to M23 per UN).

Two diplomatic tracks followed: a US-brokered DRC-Rwanda deal (signed by Tshisekedi and Kagame in Washington on 4 Dec 2025) linking Rwandan withdrawal, FDLR neutralisation and minerals investment, and Qatar-mediated DRC-M23 talks (Doha framework, 15 Nov 2025). Why it matters: the war involves at least three national armies, threatens a regional conflict with Burundi, and sits on minerals central to US supply-chain strategy.
year: M23 kept attacking despite the Washington signing: it took Lubarika (2 Dec 2025), Luvungi (4 Dec) and Sange (8 Dec) and entered Uvira on 9-10 Dec, pushing south along Lake Tanganyika to Makobola; Burundian, FARDC and Wazalendo forces fled, about 200,000 people were displaced and at least 400 were killed. Under US pressure M23 announced a pullback, and FARDC re-entered Uvira on 18 Jan 2026; 171 bodies were later found in two mass graves there. In January Rwanda's ambassador acknowledged 'security coordination' with M23 to the US Congress.

February 2026 saw the most air and drone strikes ever recorded in a month in the DRC (ACLED): FARDC used CH-4 and Anka drones, jets and helicopters, and a drone killed M23 spokesman Willy Ngoma near Rubaya on 24 Feb. M23 answered with kamikaze drones on Kisangani airport, the FARDC command hub, from 31 Jan, and counterattacked in late February. The US sanctioned the Rwandan army and four officers in March, Joseph Kabila in April and M23's intelligence chief in June; Rubio told Congress he expected Rwanda out by mid-July. M23 withdrew from the Ruzizi Plain in May. On 26 June the DRC took Rwanda to the ICJ.

From mid-August a government offensive with contractors pushed on Minembwe; on 17 Sept FRN/Twirwaneho fighters ambushed Vectus Global contractors near Mulima, wounding ex-Green Beret Tim Kennedy and killing a New Zealander. In September FARDC and Wazalendo made notable gains in southern Masisi (Kazinga, a hill near Kibabi, the Ufamandu villages) while the RP529 and RP1030 axes changed hands repeatedly. Burundian and Rwandan troops exchanged fire across the Kagera River on 5 Sept. On 12 Oct Kabila launched the FRN in Goma; the same week FRN fought a ten-day battle in the Kaziba and Walungu highlands, displacing 12,000+ households, and announced plans to march on Uvira and Kalemie.
situation: As of late October 2026 M23/FRN controls Goma, Bukavu, Rutshuru, most of Masisi and Kalehe, the Rubaya mines and the Walungu-Kamanyola area, while the government holds Uvira, the Ruzizi Plain, Walikale and the Beni-Butembo axis. Active fronts: southern Masisi near Ngungu and Rubaya, the RP529 (Kibati, Nyabiondo) and RP1030 (Minjenje, Malemo toward Pinga) axes, the Kaziba-Walungu highlands toward Kamanyola and Luvungi, and the Minembwe highlands (Point Zero, Mulima, Rugezi, Gipimo). A Doha meeting was planned for late October and AU facilitators visited Kinshasa from 8 Oct, but FRN's creation may derail talks.
technical: M23/ARC force generation: Tchanzu graduations of 9,350 (Oct 2025), 7,532 (Feb 2026) and 9,318 (about 20 July 2026); Rumangabo graduations of 7,437 (Sept 2025) and 1,518 special forces (Mar 2026) (KT Press, citing ceremony figures).
UN Group of Experts (June 2026) estimated about 30,000 M23 combatants, including former FARDC, police and militia members.

M23 long-range strike: kamikaze drones carrying submunitions against Kisangani's Bangoka airport from 31 Jan 2026 (eight drones reportedly neutralised on the first night), roughly 1,000 km from the front (Wikipedia timeline; ACLED).
One-way attack (OWA) drones are now used by both sides; FRN used them on Ufamandu (15 Oct 2026) and government forces on Mukoko, Rugezi, Point Zero and Kibati (CTP).
Government drone fleet: Chinese CH-4 and Turkish TAI Anka (ACLED); Bayraktar TB2 use alleged around Minembwe in June 2026; a Chinese CH-10 tilt-rotor drone alleged in Oct 2026 (unverified).
February 2026 was the record month for air and drone strikes in the DRC (ACLED); a FARDC drone killed M23 military spokesman Willy Ngoma near Rubaya on 24 Feb 2026.

Contractors: Vectus Global (Erik Prince) supports operations, deployed around Kalemie for about a year; ambushed near Mulima on 17 Sept 2026 (20+ casualties); Prince negotiating a ~$200m helicopter support contract (CTP, citing NYT and Africa Intelligence).

Air defence on the rebel side: Twirwaneho reportedly captured a Chinese Yitian short-range air defence system abandoned by contractors; a Russian-made Antonov cargo plane was reportedly shot down over Minembwe in late Aug 2026 (CTP, single-source).

Burundian commitment: about 18,000 FDNB troops in South Kivu before Uvira fell (CTP); about 5,000 fighting with FARDC in Feb 2026, about 4,000 in Fizi/Mwenga in Apr 2026, and up to 1,300 more deployed in May 2026 (Wikipedia timeline).

Rwandan role: the US sanctioned the RDF and four senior officers (Mar 2026); the RDF was accused of building a base at Mumosho near Bukavu (Apr 2026); Rwandan forces reportedly tracked a contractor drone before the Mulima ambush (Reuters via CTP).
M23 freed more than 5,000 captured FARDC soldiers to the ICRC at Rumangabo in early Mar 2026 (Wikipedia timeline).
Economic war: Rubaya supplies about 15% of world coltan and earns M23 at least US$800,000 a month (UN via ACLED); Kinshasa promised Rubaya to the US in a minerals deal (5 Feb 2026).
Front-line pattern: hills and villages change hands within days (Kibati changed control at least three times in Sept 2026; Minjenje several times), so control should be mapped as contested belts.
Regional escalation risk: Burundian and Rwandan troops exchanged fire near the Kagera River on 5 Sept 2026; Burundi deployed hundreds of soldiers and Imbonerakure along the border (CTP).
casualties: No consolidated toll for the window. Uvira offensive (Dec 2025): at least 400 killed (regional authorities and UN); 171 bodies found in two mass graves in Uvira (Feb 2026). ACLED: political violence in North and South Kivu rose 70% in 2025 vs 2024. Unverified claims include up to 470 government soldiers killed in Fizi in early Sept 2026 (M23-aligned outlet). A drone strike in Goma on 11 Mar 2026 killed three including a UNICEF staffer. Deaths in the window very likely exceeded 1,000 (inference from the Uvira toll and the scale of 2026 fighting).
displaced: About 200,000 displaced by the Uvira offensive (Dec 2025, Reuters headline via Wikipedia); more than 12,000 households displaced in Kaziba in Oct 2026 (Actualite.cd via CTP); new displacement waves from Masisi and Walikale in Sept 2026 (AllAfrica). Rwanda said at least 3,000 Congolese refugees had returned in 2026, with 10,000 more planned in H2 2026. No current national IDP total retrieved.

timeline.event: DRC and M23 sign the Doha framework agreement with eight protocols.
Tshisekedi and Kagame sign the Washington peace accords with Trump presiding.
FARDC re-enters Uvira after M23 withdrawal.
M23 kamikaze drones strike Kisangani airport.
FARDC drone kills M23 spokesman Willy Ngoma near Rubaya.
Montreux round of the Doha process: MoU on FARDC prisoner transfer; ceasefire monitoring expanded.
M23 withdraws from the Ruzizi Plain.
DRC files an ICJ case against Rwanda.
Burundian and Rwandan troops exchange fire near the Kagera River.
Vectus Global contractors ambushed near Mulima, South Kivu.
Joseph Kabila launches the FRN in Goma as its president.
FRN announces plans to march on Uvira and Kalemie.

outlook: Watch whether FRN attacks toward Uvira and the Ruzizi Plain, whether the late-October Doha meeting and a December round in Tanzania happen, whether Washington follows its sanctions with further pressure on Rwanda after the missed mid-July withdrawal expectation, the Burundi-Rwanda border, and the impact of the Ebola outbreak on operations in North Kivu.

zones.name: Goma and Nyiragongo (M23/FRN)
zones.note: M23 capital since Jan 2025; FRN launched here on 12 Oct 2026; drone strikes in March 2026.

zones.name: Rutshuru-Kiwanja (M23/FRN)
zones.note: M23 rear base and Tchanzu/Rumangabo training camps; Wazalendo raids near Nyamilima and Kiseguro.

zones.name: Masisi-Rubaya (contested)
zones.note: Coltan mines; Sept-Oct 2026 FARDC-Wazalendo push near Kibabi, Ngungu and Ufamandu.

zones.name: RP529 axis, Nyabiondo-Kibati (contested)
zones.note: Kibati and Mahanga changed hands repeatedly in Sept-Oct 2026.

zones.name: RP1030 axis toward Pinga (contested)
zones.note: Minjenje, Malemo, Chanjikiro and Buhimba fought over; M23 aims at Pinga and Walikale.

zones.name: Kalehe (M23 with Wazalendo pockets)
zones.note: Wazalendo retook villages near Tushunguti in Sept 2026.

zones.name: Bukavu (M23/FRN)
zones.note: Taken Feb 2025; RDF accused of building a base at nearby Mumosho.

zones.name: Walungu-Kaziba-Kamanyola highlands (contested)
zones.note: FRN offensive from 11 Oct 2026; FRN says it will march on Uvira.

zones.name: Uvira and Ruzizi Plain (government)
zones.note: Held by M23 10 Dec 2025 to Jan 2026; government since; M23 left the plain in May 2026.

zones.name: Minembwe and Itombwe highlands (contested)
zones.note: Twirwaneho vs FARDC, FDNB, Wazalendo and contractors; Point Zero, Mulima, Rugezi, Gipimo.

zones.name: Kisangani (government rear)
zones.note: FARDC command and drone hub; hit by M23 kamikaze drones from Jan 2026.

battles.name: FRN offensive in the Kaziba and Walungu highlands
battles.place: Kaziba, Muhumba, Mitimbili and Munanira, Walungu territory, South Kivu, DR Congo (coordinates approximate)
battles.outcome: Ten-plus days of fighting; FRN dislodged Wazalendo from several hills near Kaziba centre and pushed toward Kamanyola; FARDC reinforced Luvungi and Lubarika after retaking Muhungu.
battles.forces: FRN infantry with drones; FARDC drones; Wazalendo militias.
battles.losses: No figures; more than 12,000 households displaced in Kaziba (Actualite.cd via CTP).
battles.significance: First major FRN offensive after Kabila took over; FRN says its aim is Uvira and then Kalemie.

battles.name: Ambush of Vectus Global contractors near Mulima
battles.place: Mulima, near Point Zero, Minembwe highlands, South Kivu, DR Congo (coordinates approximate)
battles.outcome: Contractor column ambushed while moving to encircle Minembwe.
battles.forces: Vectus Global contractor contingent; Twirwaneho fighters.
battles.losses: At least 20 killed or wounded, including Tim Kennedy (wounded, evacuated) and New Zealander Justin Conaglen (killed). Several Colombian mercenaries killed earlier in September (NYT via CTP).
battles.significance: Exposed the Western private-military role in Kinshasa's war; Reuters reported Rwandan forces may have tracked a contractor drone to the site.

sources.label: Critical Threats: Congo War Security Review, 21 Oct 2026

battles.name: Government offensive in southern Masisi
battles.place: Kazinga, Kibabi, Ufamandu and Katoyi, Masisi, North Kivu, DR Congo (mapped near Kibabi, approximate)
battles.outcome: Government gains: Kazinga (12 Sept), hill near Kibabi (15 Sept), Katuunda, Kaleta, Miano, Muhororo, Kasake (16 Sept), Kasake, Shovu, Kawele, Nyakigano (8 Oct); M23 counterattacks continue around Ngungu and Remeka.
battles.forces: FARDC special forces and Wazalendo; M23 reinforcements from Rutshuru.
battles.losses: No reliable figures; displacement waves reported.
battles.significance: The most notable government ground gains against M23 since early 2025, pressing toward the Rubaya coltan mines.

battles.name: M23 Uvira offensive and capture of Uvira
battles.place: Uvira and the Ruzizi Plain, South Kivu, DR Congo
battles.outcome: M23 took Lubarika (2 Dec), Luvungi (4 Dec), Sange (8 Dec) and Uvira (9-10 Dec), advancing to Makobola; it withdrew under US pressure in January and FARDC returned on 18 Jan 2026.
battles.forces: M23 with 'significant Rwandan army support' (CTP); about 18,000 Burundian troops in South Kivu at the time.
battles.losses: At least 400 killed (regional authorities and UN); about 200,000 displaced; M23 said it captured several hundred Burundian soldiers; 171 bodies later found in mass graves.
battles.significance: Came days after the Washington accords were signed; took the last government stronghold in South Kivu and the gateway to Burundi, triggering the worst Burundi-Rwanda tension in years.
